mainEntity.name: Is Suboxone just trading one addiction for another?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Suboxone creates physical dependence, but taken as prescribed it does not produce a high or the compulsive, life-damaging pattern that defines addiction. It stabilizes the brain so a person can function, much like medication for other chronic conditions.

mainEntity.name: How long does Suboxone stay in your system?

acceptedAnswer.text: Buprenorphine has a long half-life of roughly 24 to 42 hours and can be detected for about 7 to 9 days after the last dose, which is why Suboxone can often be taken once daily.

mainEntity.name: How long should I stay on Suboxone?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single right answer. Some people use it for months, others for years, and some indefinitely. Longer treatment lowers the risk of relapse and overdose, so tapering should be decided with a prescriber once stable.
Overdose on Suboxone alone is much less likely than with full opioids because of buprenorphine's ceiling effect. The main danger is mixing it with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives.

Precipitated withdrawal is sudden, intense withdrawal triggered when Suboxone is taken too soon after a full opioid. Waiting until you are in mild to moderate withdrawal before the first dose prevents it.

mainEntity.name: Can I take Suboxone if I have chronic pain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sometimes. Buprenorphine has pain-relieving properties, and some people with both opioid dependence and chronic pain do well on it. It requires a prescriber who understands both issues.

mainEntity.name: Does Suboxone show up on a drug test?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard drug panels do not usually flag buprenorphine, but specific tests for it exist and are sometimes used in treatment monitoring. Ask your prescriber for documentation if needed.

mainEntity.name: Can I drink alcohol while taking Suboxone?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is strongly discouraged. Both alcohol and Suboxone can slow breathing, and combining them raises the risk of dangerous sedation. Tell your treatment team if alcohol is also a problem.

Treating opioid use disorder during pregnancy matters for both parent and baby, and buprenorphine is used in pregnancy under medical supervision. Have this conversation with your care team rather than stopping on your own.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I miss a dose of Suboxone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because buprenorphine lasts a long time, missing one dose may not cause immediate withdrawal. Take it when you remember, do not double up without guidance, and contact your prescriber if you miss several.

mainEntity.name: Can my family doctor prescribe Suboxone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. In Canada, family doctors and nurse practitioners can prescribe Suboxone, and many do. It is also available through addiction clinics and rapid access services.

mainEntity.name: How is Suboxone different from naloxone alone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Naloxone alone is an emergency medication that reverses an overdose. Suboxone uses a small amount of naloxone only as a misuse deterrent, while its active ingredient buprenorphine provides ongoing treatment.

mainEntity.name: Will I feel high on Suboxone?

acceptedAnswer.text: People dependent on opioids generally do not feel high on a proper Suboxone dose. They feel normal and stable, without withdrawal or cravings.

mainEntity.name: Can Suboxone treat addiction to prescription painkillers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Suboxone treats opioid use disorder regardless of which opioid caused it, including oxycodone, hydromorphone, and codeine.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if I think I am becoming dependent on opioids?

acceptedAnswer.text: Reach out for an assessment as early as you can. A doctor, addiction clinic, or confidential helpline can guide you toward Suboxone, detox, counseling, or a combination.

blocks.html: Suboxone Explained: How Buprenorphine-Naloxone Helps Canadians Recover From Opioid Addiction

blocks.text: If someone you love is caught in opioid addiction, you have probably heard the word Suboxone more than once. Maybe a doctor mentioned it, maybe a friend in recovery swears by it, or maybe you have read frightening things online and you are not sure what to believe. Suboxone sits at the center of how Canada treats opioid use disorder today, and understanding it can take a lot of fear out of the decision to ask for help.

Maybe a doctor mentioned it, maybe a friend in recovery swears by it, or maybe you have read frightening things online and you are not sure what to believe. Suboxone sits at the center of how Canada treats opioid use disorder today, and understanding it can take a lot of fear out of the decision to ask for help.

blocks.text: This guide walks through what Suboxone actually is, how buprenorphine and naloxone work together, who it helps, what starting it looks like, and how it fits into a complete recovery plan. It is written for families and for people thinking about treatment in Ontario and across Canada. None of it replaces a medical assessment, but it should help you walk into that first appointment knowing the right questions to ask.

blocks.text: What Is Suboxone?
blocks.html: What Is Suboxone?

blocks.text: Suboxone is a prescription medicine used to treat opioid use disorder. It combines two ingredients, buprenorphine and naloxone, in a small film or tablet that dissolves under the tongue. Health Canada has approved it for adults with moderate to severe opioid dependence, and it is now considered a first-line treatment for opioid addiction in this country.
blocks.html: Suboxone is a prescription medicine used to treat opioid use disorder. It combines two ingredients, buprenorphine and naloxone, in a small film or tablet that dissolves under the tongue. Health Canada has approved it for adults with moderate to severe opioid dependence, and it is now considered a first-line treatment for opioid addiction in this country.

blocks.text: The simplest way to think about it: Suboxone calms the brain’s demand for opioids. It eases withdrawal, quiets cravings, and lets a person feel normal enough to rebuild their life, without the dangerous highs and crashes of heroin or street fentanyl. It is one tool inside the broader category of opioid addiction treatment, and for many people it is the tool that finally makes recovery feel possible.

blocks.text: Quick answer: What is Suboxone? Suboxone is a Health Canada approved medication for opioid use disorder that combines buprenorphine, a partial opioid agonist, with naloxone, an opioid blocker. Taken under the tongue once daily, it reduces withdrawal and cravings so a person can stabilize and stay in treatment more safely than with full opioids.

Quick answer: What is Suboxone?
Suboxone is a Health Canada approved medication for opioid use disorder that combines buprenorphine, a partial opioid agonist, with naloxone, an opioid blocker. Taken under the tongue once daily, it reduces withdrawal and cravings so a person can stabilize and stay in treatment more safely than with full opioids.

blocks.text: The two ingredients
blocks.html: The two ingredients

blocks.text: Buprenorphine is the active worker in Suboxone. It attaches to the same brain receptors that heroin, fentanyl, and prescription painkillers target, but it only partially switches them on. That partial action is enough to stop withdrawal and cravings without producing a strong high.
blocks.html: Buprenorphine is the active worker in Suboxone. It attaches to the same brain receptors that heroin, fentanyl, and prescription painkillers target, but it only partially switches them on. That partial action is enough to stop withdrawal and cravings without producing a strong high.

blocks.text: Naloxone is the safeguard. It is the same medication found in overdose reversal kits. When Suboxone is taken correctly under the tongue, the naloxone is barely absorbed and does almost nothing. It is there mainly to discourage people from crushing and injecting the medicine, because if it is injected, the naloxone can trigger sudden withdrawal.

blocks.text: How it differs from the opioids it treats
blocks.html: How it differs from the opioids it treats

blocks.text: Drugs like heroin, fentanyl, and oxycodone are full opioid agonists. They fully activate opioid receptors, which is what creates the intense high and, at higher doses, the slowed breathing that causes fatal overdose. Buprenorphine is different by design. Because it only partially activates those receptors and has what doctors call a ceiling effect, the opioid effect levels off even if a person takes more. That single difference is a large part of why Suboxone is considered safer than the drugs people come to it from.

blocks.text: How Does Suboxone Work in the Brain?
blocks.html: How Does Suboxone Work in the Brain?

blocks.text: Opioid addiction is not a moral failure or a lack of willpower. Repeated opioid use rewires the brain’s reward and stress systems so that the body comes to need the drug just to feel ordinary. Take the drug away and the brain floods with withdrawal: pain, nausea, sweating, anxiety, and a craving so strong it can override almost everything else. Suboxone works by gently occupying the same receptors and keeping that system steady.

blocks.text: The partial agonist and the ceiling effect
blocks.html: The partial agonist and the ceiling effect

blocks.text: Buprenorphine binds very tightly to opioid receptors, more tightly in fact than most other opioids. Once it is in place, it both satisfies the receptor enough to stop withdrawal and blocks weaker opioids from pushing it aside. The ceiling effect means that beyond a certain dose, taking more buprenorphine does not increase the opioid effect or the risk of slowed breathing. This is why buprenorphine carries a much lower overdose risk than full opioids. One Health Canada linked review notes that buprenorphine and naloxone offer effectiveness comparable to methadone at proper doses while bringing a stronger safety profile.

blocks.text: Why naloxone is in the mix
blocks.html: Why naloxone is in the mix

blocks.text: On its own, buprenorphine is sometimes prescribed as a single ingredient tablet. The combination product adds naloxone purely as a misuse deterrent. Swallowed or dissolved under the tongue as directed, naloxone has very low bioavailability, meaning the body absorbs almost none of it. Injected, it becomes active and can bring on uncomfortable withdrawal. This clever pairing is one reason the combination is favoured for take-home prescribing. If you want to understand naloxone’s life saving role in overdoses specifically, our piece on naloxone as an overdose reversal tool goes deeper.

Injected, it becomes active and can bring on uncomfortable withdrawal. This clever pairing is one reason the combination is favoured for take-home prescribing. If you want to understand naloxone’s life saving role in overdoses specifically, our piece on naloxone as an overdose reversal tool goes deeper.

blocks.text: What Suboxone Treats
blocks.html: What Suboxone Treats

blocks.text: Suboxone is used to treat opioid use disorder, the medical term for addiction to opioids. That includes dependence on street drugs like heroin and illicit fentanyl, as well as on prescription opioids such as oxycodone, hydromorphone, morphine, and codeine. People who developed dependence through legitimate chronic pain and opioid treatment can benefit from it too, and so can those who misuse prescription drugs they were never prescribed.

blocks.text: It is not a treatment for alcohol, cocaine, or benzodiazepine addiction, although many people in recovery are dealing with more than one substance at once. When opioid addiction overlaps with another condition such as depression, anxiety, or trauma, an approach called dual diagnosis treatment addresses both at the same time, which gives recovery a much better chance of lasting.

blocks.text: Suboxone and Canada’s Opioid Crisis
blocks.html: Suboxone and Canada’s Opioid Crisis

blocks.text: To understand why Canadian doctors lean on Suboxone, it helps to see the scale of the problem. Between January 2016 and December 2025, Canada recorded 56,631 apparent opioid toxicity deaths, according to the federal government’s substance harms tracking. In 2025 alone there were 5,630 such deaths, and 96 percent of them were accidental. Fentanyl was involved in 56 percent of those deaths, which shows how poisoned and unpredictable the illegal drug supply has become.

blocks.text: There is some cautious hope in the newest numbers. Opioid deaths fell about 23 percent in 2025 after a 17 percent drop in 2024, a decline officials link to wider naloxone access, changes in the drug supply, and broader treatment. Most deaths still cluster in British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario. Against this backdrop, getting people onto a safer medication quickly is a public health priority, and that is exactly the role Suboxone plays. You can read more about the wider picture in our overview of drug rehabilitation in Canada.

blocks.text: Where Suboxone fits: opioid agonist treatment
blocks.html: Where Suboxone fits: opioid agonist treatment

blocks.text: Suboxone is the most common form of what clinicians call opioid agonist treatment, sometimes shortened to OAT. The idea is to replace a dangerous, short acting, illegally made opioid with a regulated, long acting medication taken under medical supervision. Staying engaged in this kind of treatment is linked to fewer overdoses, lower death rates, and reduced spread of HIV and hepatitis C. It is harm reduction and recovery support rolled into one.

blocks.text: Starting Suboxone: Induction and Dosing
blocks.html: Starting Suboxone: Induction and Dosing

blocks.text: The first day on Suboxone is the part that trips people up most often, so it is worth understanding clearly. Because buprenorphine binds so tightly and pushes other opioids off the receptor, taking it too soon after using a full opioid can trigger sudden, intense withdrawal. Doctors call this precipitated withdrawal, and avoiding it is the whole point of careful timing.

blocks.text: Why timing matters
blocks.html: Why timing matters

blocks.text: A person needs to already be in mild to moderate opioid withdrawal before the first dose. In practice that usually means waiting at least 6 to 12 hours after short acting opioids like heroin, and longer after long acting ones or methadone. Clinicians often use a simple withdrawal scale to judge readiness rather than the clock alone. Starting at the right moment turns Suboxone into relief. Starting too early can make someone feel much worse for a while, which is why this step is done with guidance.

blocks.text: Typical induction and maintenance
blocks.html: Typical induction and maintenance

blocks.text: Once withdrawal is established, the first dose is small and the clinician watches how the person responds, adding more in steps over the day. The dose is then settled over the following days into a single daily amount that holds cravings and withdrawal at bay. The table below shows a common pattern, though every person’s plan is individual and set by their prescriber.

blocks.text: Suboxone Versus Methadone
blocks.html: Suboxone Versus Methadone

blocks.text: Suboxone and methadone are the two main medications for opioid use disorder in Canada, and people often ask which is better. The honest answer is that the better choice depends on the person. Methadone is a full agonist with no ceiling effect, which makes it powerful for severe, long standing addiction but also riskier in overdose, especially when mixed with alcohol or benzodiazepines. Suboxone’s ceiling effect makes it safer and easier to take home, though some people with very heavy use stabilize better on methadone.

blocks.text: Is Suboxone Addictive? Dependence Versus Addiction
blocks.html: Is Suboxone Addictive? Dependence Versus Addiction

blocks.text: This is the question families worry about most, and it deserves a careful answer. Suboxone does create physical dependence. If you stop it suddenly, you will go through withdrawal, the same way you would coming off any opioid. But physical dependence is not the same thing as addiction. Addiction is a pattern of compulsive use that harms your life despite the consequences. Most people on properly prescribed Suboxone are not chasing a high. They are taking a steady dose that lets them work, parent, and function.

blocks.text: Think of it the way you might think about insulin for diabetes or medication for high blood pressure. The body relies on it, but the person’s life gets better, not worse. That said, Suboxone can be misused, particularly by people who buy it on the street to manage withdrawal when they cannot get a prescription. Misuse risk is real but far lower than with full opioids.

blocks.text: Signs Suboxone is being misused
blocks.html: Signs Suboxone is being misused

blocks.text: It helps to know the difference between taking Suboxone as prescribed and slipping into misuse. Warning signs include taking more than prescribed, using it without a prescription, combining it with other substances to amplify effects, doctor shopping, or growing preoccupation with getting the next dose. If you notice these patterns in yourself or someone else, it is a signal to talk to the prescriber rather than a reason for shame. Our guide on relapse prevention covers how to respond when warning signs appear.

blocks.text: Suboxone Withdrawal Timeline
blocks.html: Suboxone Withdrawal Timeline

blocks.text: Because Suboxone is an opioid, stopping it produces withdrawal. The good news is that buprenorphine has a long half life, so the withdrawal tends to come on more slowly and feel less sharp than withdrawal from short acting opioids like heroin. The flip side is that it can drag on a bit longer. Nobody should stop Suboxone abruptly. A gradual taper guided by a clinician is far more comfortable and far more likely to succeed.

blocks.text: Coming off Suboxone safely
blocks.html: Coming off Suboxone safely

blocks.text: There is no medal for stopping fast. Many people stay on Suboxone for a year or more, and some stay on it indefinitely, because the evidence shows that longer treatment lowers the risk of relapse and overdose. When the time is right, a slow taper combined with counseling and strong support gives the best outcome. Going through this with help, whether in a structured program or through medical detox in Canada, is much safer than trying to white knuckle it alone.

blocks.text: Suboxone Is One Part of a Full Recovery Plan
blocks.html: Suboxone Is One Part of a Full Recovery Plan

blocks.text: Medication alone can stabilize a person, but lasting recovery usually needs more. Suboxone quiets the physical pull of opioids, which frees up the mental and emotional energy to do the deeper work: understanding why the addiction took hold, repairing relationships, and building a life that does not revolve around using. The strongest results come from combining medication with counseling and ongoing support.

blocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions About Suboxone
blocks.html: Frequently Asked Questions About Suboxone

blocks.text: Is Suboxone just trading one addiction for another?
blocks.html: Is Suboxone just trading one addiction for another?

blocks.text: No. Suboxone creates physical dependence, but taken as prescribed it does not produce a high or the compulsive, life damaging pattern that defines addiction. It stabilizes the brain so a person can function, much like medication for other chronic conditions. Most people on it are living fuller, safer lives, not chasing a drug.

It stabilizes the brain so a person can function, much like medication for other chronic conditions. Most people on it are living fuller, safer lives, not chasing a drug.

blocks.text: How long does Suboxone stay in your system?
blocks.html: How long does Suboxone stay in your system?

blocks.text: Buprenorphine has a long half life of roughly 24 to 42 hours, and it can be detected for about 7 to 9 days after the last dose. This long action is part of why Suboxone can often be taken just once a day and why its withdrawal comes on slowly.
blocks.html: Buprenorphine has a long half life of roughly 24 to 42 hours, and it can be detected for about 7 to 9 days after the last dose. This long action is part of why Suboxone can often be taken just once a day and why its withdrawal comes on slowly.

blocks.text: How long should I stay on Suboxone?
blocks.html: How long should I stay on Suboxone?

blocks.text: There is no single right answer. Some people use it for several months, others for years, and some stay on it indefinitely. Research consistently shows that longer treatment lowers the risk of relapse and overdose, so the decision to taper should be made carefully with your prescriber when you feel stable.

Research consistently shows that longer treatment lowers the risk of relapse and overdose, so the decision to taper should be made carefully with your prescriber when you feel stable.

blocks.text: Can you overdose on Suboxone?
blocks.html: Can you overdose on Suboxone?

blocks.text: Overdose on Suboxone alone is much less likely than with full opioids because of buprenorphine’s ceiling effect. The real danger comes from mixing it with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives, which can slow breathing. Used as prescribed and on its own, it is considered very safe.

blocks.text: What is precipitated withdrawal?
blocks.html: What is precipitated withdrawal?

blocks.text: Precipitated withdrawal is sudden, intense withdrawal triggered when Suboxone is taken too soon after a full opioid. Buprenorphine knocks the other opioid off the receptor and only partially replaces it, causing a rapid crash. Waiting until you are in mild to moderate withdrawal before the first dose prevents it.

blocks.text: Can I take Suboxone if I have chronic pain?
blocks.html: Can I take Suboxone if I have chronic pain?

blocks.text: Sometimes. Buprenorphine does have pain relieving properties, and some people with both opioid dependence and chronic pain do well on it. This is a nuanced situation that needs a prescriber who understands both issues, since pain management and addiction treatment have to be balanced carefully.

blocks.text: Does Suboxone show up on a drug test?
blocks.html: Does Suboxone show up on a drug test?

blocks.text: Standard drug panels do not usually flag buprenorphine, but specific tests for it exist and are sometimes used in treatment monitoring. If a test could affect your job or legal situation, it is reasonable to ask your prescriber for documentation that you are taking it legitimately.

blocks.text: Can I drink alcohol while taking Suboxone?
blocks.html: Can I drink alcohol while taking Suboxone?

blocks.text: It is strongly discouraged. Both alcohol and Suboxone can slow breathing, and combining them raises the risk of dangerous sedation. If alcohol is also a problem for you, tell your treatment team so they can address both substances safely.

blocks.text: Is Suboxone safe during pregnancy?
blocks.html: Is Suboxone safe during pregnancy?

blocks.text: Treating opioid use disorder during pregnancy is important for both parent and baby, and buprenorphine is used in pregnancy under medical supervision. The single ingredient form is sometimes preferred. Anyone who is pregnant or planning to be should have this conversation with their care team rather than stopping treatment on their own.

blocks.text: What happens if I miss a dose?
blocks.html: What happens if I miss a dose?

blocks.text: Because buprenorphine lasts a long time, missing one dose may not cause immediate withdrawal, but you should take it as soon as you remember and contact your prescriber if you miss several. Do not double up without guidance. Consistency keeps cravings and withdrawal under control.

blocks.text: Can my family doctor prescribe Suboxone?
blocks.html: Can my family doctor prescribe Suboxone?

blocks.text: Yes. In Canada, family doctors and nurse practitioners can prescribe Suboxone, and many do. You can also access it through addiction clinics and rapid access services. This wide availability is one reason it has become a first-line treatment.

blocks.text: How is Suboxone different from naloxone alone?
blocks.html: How is Suboxone different from naloxone alone?

blocks.text: Naloxone alone, found in overdose reversal kits, is an emergency medication that quickly blocks opioids to reverse an overdose. Suboxone uses a small amount of naloxone only as a misuse deterrent, while its active ingredient buprenorphine provides ongoing treatment. They serve very different purposes.

blocks.text: Will I feel high on Suboxone?
blocks.html: Will I feel high on Suboxone?

blocks.text: People who are dependent on opioids generally do not feel high on a proper Suboxone dose. Instead they feel normal and stable, without withdrawal or cravings. Someone with no opioid tolerance might feel effects, which is one reason it is prescribed and monitored carefully.

blocks.text: Can Suboxone be used to treat addiction to prescription painkillers?
blocks.html: Can Suboxone be used to treat addiction to prescription painkillers?

blocks.text: Yes. Suboxone treats opioid use disorder regardless of which opioid caused it, including prescription medications like oxycodone, hydromorphone, and codeine. People who became dependent through pain treatment can benefit just as much as those who used street opioids.

blocks.text: What should I do if I think I am becoming dependent on opioids?
blocks.html: What should I do if I think I am becoming dependent on opioids?

blocks.text: Reach out for an assessment as early as you can. The sooner opioid use disorder is treated, the better the outcomes. A doctor, an addiction clinic, or a confidential helpline can guide you toward the right next step, whether that is Suboxone, detox, counseling, or a combination.

blocks.text: The Bottom Line
blocks.html: The Bottom Line

blocks.text: Suboxone is not a magic cure, and it is not a crutch to be ashamed of. It is a safe, evidence based medication that has helped thousands of Canadians step back from the edge of the opioid crisis and start rebuilding. By easing withdrawal and quieting cravings, it buys people the stability they need to do the real work of recovery. Paired with counseling, family support, and a plan for the long term, it gives opioid addiction a genuine path forward.
